title: The editorial policy is now public
change: First published: the standards, the levels of evidence we accept, and the source details recorded behind every claim on this site.
reason: So you can see the rules a page was written to before you decide whether to rely on it.

title: The privacy page is now public
change: First published, and written to match what the site really does: no analytics, no cookies, and anything you type into a tool stays only in your own browser.
reason: A privacy page written for how the site actually works, not for one still being planned.

title: No Colombia destination page yet
change: Not created. A destination page for Colombia is planned, but no source behind the usual claims is sound enough to publish.
reason: The citation repeated across provider sites is wrong. Colombia's Constitutional Court ruling on a surrogacy arrangement is T-968 of 2009, not 2014; the court's T-968/2014 document is about disability rating. The 2009 decision is a tutela about custody and contact for twins, and it says only that there is no express prohibition, which is narrower than the way it is usually described. The full text needs reading before anything is written from it.

title: No India, Ukraine or Portugal destination pages yet
supersededBy: Destination pages for four more jurisdictions
change: Not created.
reason: India: the ICMR page listing the 2021 Acts and Rules is reachable, but its substantive provisions could not be retrieved from any official source, so eligibility details, insurance amounts and offence sections cannot be published. Ukraine and Portugal: every statutory text we tried either failed to load or turned out to be an agency's marketing page. A page resting on a broker's summary is no better than no page at all.

title: How we handle cost figures
change: US cost figures appear only as attributed, dated, self-reported ranges from named providers, and no average is presented as a fact.
reason: There is no independent, audited or government cost dataset for surrogacy in the United States, and every usable figure traces back to a provider's own page or to an academic sentence citing one.

title: No registry statistics are quoted
change: No official registry statistic about surrogacy programs, matching, payments or outcomes is cited anywhere on this site.
reason: US assisted reproduction surveillance counts treatment cycles. There is no national registry of surrogacy agreements, compensation or program outcomes, so a claim of that kind would have no source to point you to.

title: The cost guide is now public
change: First published: the parts a cost is made of, common exclusions, escrow and refund mechanics, and the cost figures labelled by their source type.
reason: It is the main cost page, and the one every cost article points back to.

title: The process guide is now public
change: First published: nine stages, who is answerable at each, and what intended parents are expected to prepare.
reason: It lays out the framework the destination and agency guides rely on, using FIGO's 2025 guidance as the standard.

title: The agency guide is now public
change: First published: what an agency fee covers, the documents to ask for before a deposit, and questions grouped by which professional answers them.
reason: It is written around credentials rather than praise, including the difference between charity registration and regulation.

title: The legal considerations guide is now public
change: First published: enforceability, parentage, eligibility and payment kept apart as four separate questions, plus whether the country you live in will recognise the arrangement.
reason: Most destination advice collapses these four into one, whether a country 'allows surrogacy', and that is exactly where plans fall apart.

title: Explainer: why no average cost exists
change: First published.
reason: It explains what registry data does and does not cover, so you can judge any cost figure you meet elsewhere.

title: Explainer: costs outside a quote
change: First published.
reason: The exclusions list is the real gap between a quoted fee and a budget you can actually spend.

title: Explainer: escrow and payment stages
change: First published.
reason: Escrow timing decides how much of your money is at risk, and how soon, well before the headline fee does.

title: Explainer: comparing destinations
change: First published, marked as framework evidence because it asserts no external facts.
reason: It hands you a source hierarchy to apply, which is the difference between comparing for yourself and being sold to.

title: Destination pages for five jurisdictions
change: The United States, United Kingdom and Canada are published with sourced positions. Colombia and Greece are published but marked as insufficient.
reason: We show Colombia and Greece as researched but thin rather than hiding them, because the Colombia citation problem and the wrong Greek statute number are themselves useful information for you.

title: The gamete and surrogate options guide is now public
change: First published, as framework evidence. Whose egg, whose sperm and who carries the pregnancy are separated into three decisions, with what each one adds to your question list and the order in which they narrow the destination and the budget.
reason: This was the only one of the six questions on the homepage with no page answering it. Nothing here could be cited to a source worth relying on, so the page teaches you the questions and names who owes each answer instead of asserting rules.

title: The destination research checklist is now public
change: First published: thirty-three questions across eligibility, parentage, nationality, medical scope, money, presence and disputes, each carrying a status and a named source for its answer, and exportable as a document you can take with you.
reason: Every guide and article had been pointing its next step at the single tool that existed, which made that next step a formality rather than an answer. The checklist holds questions only, and makes no claim about what any particular country requires.

title: The agency question checklist is now public
change: First published: the questions to put to an agency in writing before you sign, grouped by fee scope, money and exit, the surrogate's own position, medical limits, legal work, failure, and claims you can check.
reason: A written answer can be read again against a contract, while a spoken one cannot. Nothing is submitted anywhere, and no agency is named or rated.

title: Text that was unreadable on a dark background
change: On the guides index, the quote tool page, and the outlined buttons across the site, body text and button labels were so faint against the dark background that you could barely read them. That text is now legible in both the light and the dark view.
reason: One brand colour was being used for two different jobs at once, filling a band and standing out as text, and it could not do both on a dark background. Switching the palette from navy to green uncovered the problem, which had been there all along.

title: No consultation service is offered
change: The header button, the sidebar on the content pages and the closing panel on the homepage now point you to the tools. The assessment page keeps what it says about its coverage and its limits, and moves to the footer, labelled as a page about a service that is not open.
reason: This site was being made as research and tools only. A prominent button that implied a way to reach us when none exists is exactly the kind of confident wording this site sets out to distrust.

title: Wide tables no longer drag the whole page sideways on phones
change: Three guides were wider than a phone screen, so the whole page slid sideways when you tried to reach the end of a table. Every table in the site's writing now scrolls inside its own frame, and one button label on the homepage was shortened because its unbreakable text was forcing the page too wide.
reason: A wide comparison table is how this site normally shows a difference, so on a phone the page had to choose between cramped columns and dragging everything across. We found it by checking the pages at narrow screen widths, which none of them had been checked at before.

title: The exported checklist now reads the way the rest of the site does
change: In the document you download, the status and the answer were joined by a dash the rest of this site never uses. The line now reads: Question (Confirmed: who answered it, and when).
reason: That exported document is something you take to a lawyer, and this site produces it, so a style rule that stops at the page's edge is not much of a rule. Once we saw the mismatch we made the export follow the same wording as everything else.

title: We now do take enquiries
change: The homepage now ends in a way to send us an enquiry, so there is a channel to reach us after all, and the entry above it is reversed. What has not changed is the boundary that reversal was written to protect: the assessment page still describes what it covers, still refuses legal conclusions and medical opinions, and still lists what has not been settled about the service. The main navigation now points at the four topics that block a decision and at the explainer index, and the privacy page describes the enquiry form the way it actually works.
reason: The operator intends to answer enquiries, which is a different fact from the one recorded above, and that earlier entry was written for a research-only plan. Rather than rewrite the older entry in place, which would leave this log describing a plan the site no longer follows, both entries stand and this newer one names the older one.

title: An enquiry form that sends nothing to us
change: Five fields, none of them asking who you are: where you are in the process, what is in view, who holds the document now, your question, and a reply address. The message is shown to you on the page before it goes anywhere, and the three ways to send it are your own mail app, the clipboard, or a downloaded file. Your draft is kept in this browser, so it survives a reload. The mail option only appears once a real reply inbox is set; until then the page tells you the address is missing rather than opening an empty compose window.
reason: There is nowhere on this site for a form submission to go, and a form that reports success after sending to nothing is exactly the confident wording this site exists to distrust. So the form composes the message for you and leaves the sending to you, which also keeps an enquiry from sitting on a third-party service that would hold your fertility and family details.

title: The homepage now follows one decision path
change: The homepage now runs in a single order: the four questions that block a decision, where you are starting from, the six things to verify before choosing, cost and contract weighed against information standards as two separate panels, then the reading and the enquiry form. Every module links only to a page that is real and live; a topic whose sources are unfinished shows you that it is withheld rather than a dead link.
reason: The page has to carry you from a question to a verifiable answer, so the sections follow the order in which the questions actually narrow each other, not the order in which the content was written.

title: The headline over the opening photograph is now easy to read
change: On the homepage's opening photograph, the small helper text and the second line were hard to read, especially on a phone, because the brightest part of the image sat behind them. We added a second soft layer behind the text and stopped using the faintest text colour over the photograph, so the words now stand clear against the image.
reason: A translucent overlay cannot promise readable text, because it sits on top of whatever the image happens to be. We sized the layers from the actual picture, not from how dark its preview looked.

title: Secondary text on a light background was too faint
change: The smaller, lighter text on the pale band near the top of the homepage sat just under the level where it stays easy to read, in the light view. That text is now dark enough to read comfortably, everywhere it appears.
reason: That band gained body text in this round of changes, and text a shade too light to read is a fault the new section revealed rather than one it created.

title: Three long button labels made the page scroll sideways
change: The buttons and text links on this site never wrap onto a second line, so three long labels, 'Read the cost and contract guide', 'Open the verification checklists' and 'Learn about the assessment service', forced the homepage to slide sideways on smaller screens. The labels are now shorter, and the page fits at every phone width.
reason: A label is the widest thing in its column, so the wording is part of the layout. We found the sideways slide by looking at the page at each screen width.

title: The enquiry you copy by hand was missing a reply address
change: The preview on the page wrote four lines and left your reply address out, while the clipboard and file options added it. So if your browser would not let us copy for you and you copied the preview yourself, you got an enquiry nobody could reply to. The same single message is now used by the preview, the email text, the clipboard and the file, and your reply address appears whenever you have entered one.
reason: Four ways of sending that showed your message differently meant three of them described a version you never actually saw. We checked it by filling the form in a browser ourselves, including the copy paths that are blocked or that fail.

title: Links and labels were too faint to read on two coloured bands
change: The rust colour we use for links and small labels was only ever checked against the plain backgrounds. On two of the tinted bands it came out too faint to read. The colour is now deepened so links and labels read clearly on those bands too, and where the change spoiled a hover effect we fixed that, so buttons show a readable label colour on hover and footer links mark a hover with an underline instead of a colour change.
reason: A colour picked for one background has to be readable on every background it lands on. The two tinted bands were added after the colour was chosen, and the first check only covered the obvious pairings, so they slipped through.

title: The opening photograph was behind the wrong kind of layer
change: An earlier fix left the homepage's opening photograph under a dark layer. The reasoning was sound, in that a dark layer over a sunlit sea has to overpower the brightest part of the picture, but it was the wrong layer to begin with. The page this site was designed to match is bright: the photograph reads as weather and light, with the type set in green over it. So the dark layer is now a light one, the text sits on tones that keep it readable, and below the desktop width the photograph keeps its own plain band as before.
reason: A layer has to be chosen for the photograph and for the colour scheme at the same time, and fixing only the first produces something that measures well but looks like nothing that was designed. The honest way to correct the earlier entry is to say its reasoning pointed at the wrong thing.

title: The homepage's busy background was simplified
change: Three pale background colours were competing on the homepage at once: the warm tone of the text area, a beige panel, and a sand-coloured band behind the verification section, and beige against warm looked muddled rather than deliberate. The page now sits in one tone and breaks it once, with a single cool grey-green band before the closing call to action. The verification section's sand fill is now plain with a rule above and below. The sand colour is still used elsewhere, on the region comparison tables and the source banners.
reason: Two similar warm colours side by side read like a mistake, and the only way to tell them apart at a glance is to make one of them cool. Nothing about readability changed; the tones were set against the text and links that sit on them.

title: The homepage now uses real photographs
change: Fourteen photographs replace the illustrative images on the opening panel, the four concern cards, the three stage cards, both verification panels and the four featured articles. Every card that used to carry just an icon now has a photograph above its text. The featured list shifted with it, so two of its four places now hold the legal-considerations and agency guides, because the photographs supplied actually fit those two subjects, and the escrow article is still reached from the contract panel below. One supplied image, a decorative leaf strip beside the assessment band, sits in the outer margin and so only appears on wide screens.
reason: A photograph of a harbour is not the same as a photograph of a passport, and the earlier rule against putting people in the imagery was ours, not the brief's. Where an image and its place disagreed, we moved the place.

title: A person is in the opening photograph now
change: The photograph behind the homepage's opening text replaces the earlier picture with no people in it. It shows a sunlit coast with a figure in the right third, so two things changed together: the framing was set to keep the open water behind the text and the figure clear of it, and the soft layer behind the text was redone so the headline stays readable while the sea still shows. On smaller screens the layer is dropped entirely and the photograph keeps its own plain band.
reason: The rule against putting people in the imagery was ours, not the brief's. Once a bright sea sits behind the text, a dark layer would have to hide almost the whole picture to keep the type readable, so we switched to a light layer that only lifts the darkest part behind the sentences, which is the headland.

title: The destination assessment: ten questions that give you a research roadmap
change: The destination page now opens its own tool instead of pointing you at a contact form. Three steps, ten questions, nine of them required, covering your family situation and legal identity, what you are trying to settle, and your practical conditions. Nationality, residence and marital status are asked as three separate questions, because each answers a different legal test and none stands in for another. The genetic question is optional and asks for a plan rather than a diagnosis. The budget question asks how you relate to cost and never for an amount, an income or proof of funds. Nothing asks for a name, contact details, documents or medical records. What you get back is a roadmap: the three questions every route has to answer, then up to eighteen notes that narrow against your answers, each with the live page to open next and the four parties who own each kind of answer. The tool will not name a country as suitable, because the sourced material here describes how a legal system works, not which family may use it. Three of the notes quote a legal source, each with its publisher and the date we read it. The sources are the American Society for Reproductive Medicine state survey for the US restriction, the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act route as recorded for the United Kingdom, and the Assisted Human Reproduction Act regulations for the Canadian expense reimbursement.
reason: A form that ends in 'thanks, we will be in touch' tells you nothing and gives you no reason to come back. The version worth making answers the question you actually asked, then hands the rest to the people who can settle it. An enquiry stays available as a next step, not as the outcome.

title: The assessment showed only three of its ten questions
change: The assessment kept some steps out of sight unless a page element could hide them, so in any browser that did not run that element you saw only step one, next to text promising all ten questions were on the page. Every step now shows; one control steps through them, and taking that control away leaves all ten questions visible rather than hiding any of them. The same holds for the roadmap: without that control all eighteen notes and the download option appear instead of a blank space.
reason: The header promised ten questions before the page delivered them. And because this site says plainly that its tools keep your data in your browser, that promise is only believable if the tool still works when something on your browser does not run as usual.

title: The site is designed to be bilingual, and says nothing until the Chinese pages are ready
change: A Chinese version of the whole site is being made alongside the English one, not instead of it. Every English page keeps the web address and the wording it already had, and the Chinese pages will sit under /zh with their own titles, dates, reading times, table headings and tool labels. Two visible things follow. A language switch appears in the header, and each page cross-links to its counterpart, but only on a page whose translation is actually finished, so today the English site shows neither; you will not see either on a page until its Chinese version is ready, and the pairing is not announced while any page of the mirror is still unfinished. Comparing the site before and after this change, all 34 pages came out the same apart from two small typographic tidy-ups, a sentence split across two lines being joined back into one and the copyright mark shown as its proper character, with no difference in any title or page summary.
reason: A cross-reference pointing at a page that does not exist would tell a search engine that two different pages are one, which is worse than saying nothing, and a half-translated mirror is the same mistake shown straight to you. Both are avoided by making the switch and the cross-link depend on the translated page actually existing.

title: The homepage follows the layout its owner defined
change: The homepage was made to the section order the owner set out: an opening with two calls to action, who we are against four strengths, four service cards, a row of country cards, the guides and articles, and a dark green enquiry band holding a five field form. The header now reads Home, Destinations, Services, Guides and About us, with a consultation button at the end. Three things in the plan were not adopted. A card for Georgia has no sourced record, so the row carries the five countries that do, each showing the date its sources were last opened or the words 'sources incomplete'. A stated response time is a promise this site cannot keep yet, because no enquiry address is set, so the line under the heading says what the form demonstrably does instead. A submit button that reports success would mislead when there is nothing to receive the message, so the button assembles the enquiry on screen, you read it, and it leaves through your own mail app, clipboard or a downloaded file. Three sections from the previous version are gone from the homepage: the four blocking questions, the six step research order, and the panel that kept cost, contract and liability apart. Their pages are unchanged and still reached from the cards above. The structured enquiry tool moved to the assessment page, where the service it feeds is described.
reason: The owner defined the page, so the page follows that definition rather than the earlier layout. What did not move is the rule that this site only makes a claim where it can be checked. Where the two met, the plan kept everything except the three items that would have printed a fact the record does not hold.

title: The Chinese mirror is open on all thirty-three pages
change: All thirty-three pages that have a Chinese version now cross-reference their counterpart, carry a link in the header to the same page in the other language, and are listed together for search engines. The switch was opened for all thirty-three at once, when the last Chinese page was ready. One page is deliberately left out of the mirror: the error page stays English only, because the same error document is served for every missing address and cannot know which language to answer in.
reason: The switch was withheld while any page was untranslated, and not for tidiness. A language link that lands on a missing page is worse than no language link, and a cross-reference pointing at nothing makes a search engine treat two documents as one. The promise is only made when every page in it actually exists.

title: Four new explainers fill the two empty categories
change: We added four explainers: one on the six-month limit inside a United Kingdom parental order, one on what the 40,177 transfer study measures and what it does not, one on getting a birth certificate accepted by another country's authorities, and one on the five documents that should exist before a first transfer. Each has its Chinese mirror too, so the site now carries seventy-five pages rather than sixty-seven, and the two category pages that used to show nothing now show a list.
reason: The explainer index promised five categories and four pages existed in only three of them. Trimming the promise was the cheaper fix and the wrong one, because the process and preparation topics are where a decision actually gets made, and a research site that only covers cost and destinations is describing the quote rather than the choice. So the gap was filled from sources instead of narrowed. Nothing went in that could not be traced to a page which opened; a statutory section and one consular procedure page were both dropped when they refused to load, and the transfer article reports no number of attempts per person because the study publishes none.

title: The homepage reading row now answers the three questions it names
change: The four cards in the homepage reading section are now the explainer on cost lines outside a quote, the guide on choosing an agency, the explainer on the six-month limit inside a United Kingdom parental order, and the explainer on getting a birth certificate accepted abroad. Those four answer what the section's own sentence promises. A card that a language cannot fill is filled from that language's newest pages, and the fallback wording no longer describes a pile of withheld material.
reason: The section said it held the answers to how to read a quote, what to ask a provider, and what parentage and nationality turn on, while the cards under it were chosen before two of those questions had a page of their own. A row of cards that does not match the sentence above it reads as a template, and after promising you an answer we should not show you a note about what is missing.

title: The services cards no longer offer to review your documents
change: The card that read 'What to verify in a provider or a contract' is gone. In its place the services row is destination research, costs and budget planning, one-to-one consultation, and the question list for the meetings you already have. The consultation card and the section button both go to the assessment page, where the enquiry is composed in your own browser. The assessment page still states its limit in its own place: the output is a structured written read of the documents you hold, each gap named with the party who has to close it, and 'What an assessment never does' records that we do not perform the verification.
reason: A limitation belongs on the page that describes the service, not on a homepage card whose job is to make someone want to talk to us. Selling a review of contracts or a check on a provider was already off the table, since neither needs our reading skill but a licence and the ability to act in a jurisdiction; what is left to offer is the conversation that turns a pile of documents into a list of questions with names against them.

title: The main navigation now opens on the explainer index, not the homepage
change: The first header item is now the explainer index. The wordmark keeps the homepage, so no page lost its only entry point and none gained a second one.
reason: Home is the page you are already standing on, so that slot described the navigation instead of offering you somewhere to go. The index of narrow, sourced answers was the one first-visit destination the header never carried.

title: The short-source pages are renamed from articles to explainers
change: Every word this site shows you for this kind of page now reads 'Explainers', in both languages: the header and footer links, the badge on a card, the index and category headings with their explanatory text, the breadcrumb, the related-content counts on a guide, the homepage reading row, the 404 links, and the line in the research standards that names what those standards apply to. The four publication records that opened with the old name were retitled. What is unchanged is invisible to you, so we left it alone.
reason: 'Article' is the word provider marketing already uses for a page of unsourced copy, so the label invited you to file these pages in the category where they are hardest to tell apart. 'Explainer' says what a page does: one question, the sources beneath it, the date those sources were opened. The site has no live host, no inbound link and no indexed page yet, so the wording you see could be moved now without a redirect.

title: Colombia and Greece records completed
change: Both destination records were re-sourced and no longer carry the 'sources incomplete' marking. For Colombia, we read two Constitutional Court judgments from the court's own site: T-275 of 2022, which extended maternity leave to the genetic father of a child born through a surrogacy arrangement and records that at least sixteen bills since 1998 have been introduced without one passing, and T-127 of 2024, which held that children born this way may not be discriminated against for the method of their birth, reiterated the exhorto that Congress regulate the subject, and urged a bill on civil-registration effects so the woman who lends her womb is not registered as the biological mother. The law-firm blog entry was dropped. For Greece, we read the Government Gazette text of Law 3305/2005 directly from the copy published by the national health insurer: the definition at article 3 paragraph 9, the conditions and the without-any-consideration rule at article 13, the penal provision at article 26 paragraph 8. A 2024 university thesis supplied the Civil Code articles on which parentage turns, and the May 2025 amendment requiring permanent residence of both the intending parents and the surrogate is recorded from law firm accounts and flagged as unconfirmed against the gazette.
reason: Both records were marked insufficient because the primary documents had not been found, and the documents were findable: the Colombian court publishes its own judgments, and the Greek statute sits on a government site. What remains genuinely unsettled, Colombia's regulatory gap and the exact wording of Greece's 2025 amendment, is now set out inside sourced columns instead of standing in for the whole page.

title: Header and opening panel: language dropdown, softer corners, the owner note inside the text
change: The header language switch is now a dropdown listing both languages, with the current one marked and a language with no translation of this page shown dimmed rather than clickable. Every corner on the site softened from 2px to 8px, and cards and panels to 12px. The owner's line in the opening panel, previously a tilted bordered card floating over the photograph at the bottom right, is now a single display line inside the text column under the opening paragraph.
reason: The owner reviewed the homepage and found the boxed note abrupt against a sunlit photograph, and the square corners unfinished beside the round icon frames the site already uses. The dropdown opens before anything else so no language link is hidden behind the code that runs when the page loads.

title: Copy that described the visitor in the third person now speaks to you
change: The homepage reading section opened with a line about what people read before a first conversation; it now names the three questions the section answers, and its heading was rewritten the same way. The remaining third-person references became direct address: an explainer's closing note, a guide's line about how a sentence that a country is permissive is actually heard, the empty view on the explainer index, the next-steps block on the assessment page, the bottom of the roadmap file, and two field notes on the research standards page. The Chinese tagline now addresses families rather than describing them.
reason: Pages that talk about you in the third person read like internal notes published by mistake, and the owner flagged one on the homepage. This log is a record about the site itself, so it speaks to you directly now rather than describing you in the third person.

title: Canada's record-keeping period corrected to six years
change: Four places repeated that a reimbursement file needs receipts and records kept for five years. Health Canada’s guidance and the Assisted Human Reproduction Regulations both say six years, and every mention now reads six, including the Canada destination record.
reason: A number quoted from a document has to match the document, including when the document says something less tidy than the summary did.

title: The budget components are no longer counted wrongly
change: The article said the cost guide names nine payees. Its component table has eight rows, so the sentence now describes a list of payees, each with a named biller, and leaves the counting to the table.
reason: A count that does not match the table it points at trains a reader not to check the citation.

title: The imagery statement now matches the images on this site
change: The policy said all illustration here is generated still-life imagery of documents, paper and desk objects. Several pictures show aircraft, coastlines and towns, and one shows people seen from behind. The section now states what the set contains, keeps the reason no family is photographed, and says plainly that nothing here is a photograph of anyone’s real situation.
reason: The standards page is the one page you can check against every other page on this site, and this claim did not survive that check.

title: Pages stopped describing how the site is built
change: The privacy, terms, about and assessment pages, and the enquiry forms, carried sentences written for whoever maintains this site: file paths, the names of configuration keys, endpoints, build vocabulary, and notes about what had to be filled in before launch. Those are gone. Where a decision is still open, the page now says what you are missing instead of what the build is waiting for.
reason: An internal note left on a public page reads as an accident, and it makes the honest admissions sitting next to it look like the same kind of leftovers.

title: This log is written to you, not about the build
change: Every entry was re-read, and the ones that described rendering, build steps, design variables or internal file names were rewritten as what changed for you and why. Dates, kinds, page links and the substance of each entry are unchanged.
reason: A record of what changed on a site is only useful to the people the changes affect.

title: The enquiry form no longer answers on your behalf
change: The stage and answer-holder menus start empty instead of arriving with an option pre-selected, the two fields that must be filled are marked as required, and copy or download no longer refuse a finished draft over the shape of the reply address; that check now runs only on the mail button. The assembled message skips the lines you left empty rather than writing blanks into it.
reason: A pre-selected option is a statement you did not make, inside a message that goes out under your name.

title: The quote tool states its units and saves what you typed
change: One currency covers the whole table, so the selector now says that a quote drawn up in another currency has to be converted before it is entered. Totals print in the language of the page you are on, the download is labelled as the data behind the comparison rather than a finished document, and an amount that is not a plain number is reported as unreadable instead of dropped.
reason: Two totals subtracted from each other mean nothing unless both sides are in the same currency, and a saved file you cannot read is not a deliverable.

title: The destinations index points at the records instead of repeating them
change: The comparison table on the index now shows destination, legal basis and the date each record was last checked. The payment rules stay on each record page, where their sources are quoted. The heading over the assessment tool asks what you should verify before you choose a destination, because that tool returns a roadmap of questions and never names a country as suitable for you.
reason: An answer the length of a paragraph is unreadable inside a table cell, and a heading that promises destinations the tool will not name sets the page up to miss the thing it advertises.

title: Visitor-facing Chinese now uses one form of address
change: Pages, tools, forms and the entries in this log were swept so that the reader is addressed with the formal second person throughout. The Chinese pages had mixed the formal and the casual form.
reason: Two registers on one site read as two authors who have not spoken to each other, and the casual form is the wrong one to use while a family is deciding about a child.

title: The tool index describes the checklists as they are built
change: The agency question checklist card listed five groups, including two that do not exist in the tool. It now names the seven it actually has, and the destination checklist card lists all seven areas that checklist covers instead of six.
reason: A card that previews how a page is built is a promise that page has to keep.

title: The homepage speaks to you instead of naming its audience
change: The opening line, the one-line description under it and the paragraph headed Who we are all named the people this site is for in the third person: intended parents around the world. They now say what you can do here. The one-line description exists once in each language, and the footer and the about page both read that copy.
reason: A line that names its audience is written for whoever is sizing the site up as a product. The family who opened the homepage is that audience, so the sentence was describing them to themselves.

title: The imagery paragraph on the editorial policy addresses you now
change: Its closing sentence said a borrowed stock image leaves the reader looking at a face that belongs to nobody in the story. It now says you. The revision date shown on that page moved to the day this changed.
reason: That paragraph explains a choice made for the person reading it, so the third person turned the one sentence talking to you into an observation about someone else.

title: One enquiry form, not two ways to answer questions
change: The assessment service page carried its own form beside the button that leads to the homepage enquiry. The extra one is gone. The homepage form is now the only place on this site that asks anything of you, and every other exit leads to it. The quote comparison keeps saving to your own browser as before, and every tool exit stays copy, download and your own mail app.
reason: Two forms for one act asked two different sets of questions, so the choice in front of you was about which form to fill rather than about what you needed answered.

title: The privacy page describes the form that is actually on the site
change: Its enquiry-form entry listed the fields of the form that has just been removed, including the line that no name is asked for. It now lists what the homepage form actually asks, says which one of those is optional, and says plainly that a name and a reply address are collected there when you give them.
reason: The page that tells you what gets collected has to match the boxes that are really on the site, or it is misleading in exactly the section written to prevent that.

title: The enquiry form asks three things, not five
change: The two opening menus are gone: the one that asked which stage you are at, and the one that asked for a budget band. The form now asks for a reply address, the question you want worked out, and a name to be addressed by, which is the only optional field. The mail draft and the file it composes carry the same three.
reason: Those two menus sorted an enquiry into a folder. They asked you to summarise your own situation before you had asked anything, and a cross-border plan rarely sits inside one band. What a reply needs is the question, so the form asks for the question.

title: The destination questions are a section of the page, not a quiz
change: The ten-question flow under the destination table is gone, and what it produced is printed there instead: the notes on what to verify first, each one sourced and each one naming who settles it, beside the four parties those answers belong to. Copy and download are kept, and the file they write is assembled from those notes on the page.
reason: Answering ten questions before reading anything is work done for the site rather than for your decision, and the summary it produced was the same set of notes the page could show you directly, with their sources attached.

title: The two checklists are question lists you download
change: The status menu, the answer box and the progress line beside every question are gone from both checklists, along with the buttons that added questions of your own. Each page prints its questions in seven groups, thirty-three on the destination list and thirty-one on the agency one, with one download button above them. The file arrives with an empty box beside every question.
reason: The length of the list was the argument for a checklist and then the argument against finishing one. Reading a question and downloading it costs nothing; setting a status and writing a note beside sixty-four lines is a second piece of work, and the same record kept in the downloaded file is the one a lawyer can be handed.

title: Every sentence about the tools now matches what they do
change: The tools index, the two checklist cards, the closing lines of the checklists themselves, the guide and explainer endings that told you to write your answers into a checklist, and the privacy wording around all of it have been rewritten. What the site now describes is one workspace that keeps its rows in this browser, two question lists that download, and one enquiry form.
reason: Changing what a tool does is only finished when every sentence pointing at it says the same thing. Otherwise the site’s own description is the part that misleads, and it is the part you read before deciding whether to open the tool at all.

title: The destinations page describes your comparison, not the table behind it
change: Three headings named the research file instead of the research: it asked for "the ten columns a comparison needs", for questions to be answered "before a shortlist", and for "where to go after this page". They now read "the ten things a destination comparison has to cover", "five questions to answer before you shortlist a destination", and "where to go next", and the two paragraphs underneath no longer describe empty cells in a table this page never shows. The same check ran across the site in both languages. One wording now covers each idea that was written two ways: a candidate destination, a genetic link, an escrow account, a gestational arrangement, and this site talking about itself.
reason: A heading that names columns you have never been shown makes the page sound as if it is addressing whoever maintains it. The shape of the data behind a page is not one of the things you are comparing, so it does not belong in the words read before a comparison is made.

title: A source record is described by what each part does, not by its key
change: The table under "What a source record contains" printed the six names the data is stored under, in a monospace font, and the sentence after it opened with the word "field" used in its programming sense. Both languages now list the same six parts as the citation line, the link, the publisher, when it was published, when it was checked, and what it supports, and the closing sentence reads as a sentence.
reason: This page states the standard a source has to meet, so it is the page most likely to be read by a lawyer or a regulator, and the one where the difference between a document and a database is least excusable. Storage keys belong in the file; what belongs on the page is what each part is for and why it can go stale.

title: A guide to bringing your child home after the birth
change: First published: the three documents a child has to hold at once, why the parentage order is a court step that arrives after the birth, where a genetic link is demanded and where a gestational one is accepted, the settled-abroad test that decides whether a consulate issues a travel document or asks for a visa, the two articles of the Nationality Law that leave a child with no election at eighteen, and what a local registration office asks for.
reason: This is the stretch of an arrangement that no quote covers and no provider decides, and it is the stretch where families discover they are short of time. Two of the official sources behind it refused automated retrieval, so they are marked in the source list as read from archived copies.

title: The site publishes a contents list, a feed, and dated sitemap entries
change: A list of every page in each language for a machine reader, an RSS feed of guides and explainers for each language with a link to it in the footer, a last-modified date for each sitemap entry taken from the date the sources behind that page were opened, and breadcrumb markup on every page. All four are generated from the records the pages already render from, so no claim is written a second time.
reason: A reader who wants to keep up with the site should be able to subscribe rather than remember, and an index should be able to see which pages were checked when instead of inferring it from a URL.

title: Destination pages for four more jurisdictions
change: Four records join the five already published, covering destinations this market returns to constantly. Georgia is published with a sourced position: the statute opens a surrogacy contract to a man and a woman who are married, or have lived together, for at least a year, draws no distinction between citizens and foreigners, and stays silent on payment rather than permitting it. Ukraine is published with a sourced position as well, and that includes the bill registered in August 2026 which would bar foreign customers if it were ever enacted; it is a proposal, not yet law. Kazakhstan is published as closed to international intended parents, on the family law amendment signed in July 2026. Kyrgyzstan is published and marked as incomplete, because the articles that would set the terms of a surrogacy agreement could not be opened, so that record states what the statute names and goes no further. Where an official text was not readable, the sources on each record say what they are and why they were used instead.
reason: The destinations an agent sells hardest are the ones you most need a sourced answer about, and a page that stays quiet on four of them looks exactly like a page that checked them and found nothing to write. Saying which of the four was read, and how far that reading went, is the part that is useful to you.

title: Cost figures now sit on the destination records
change: Nine destination records carry a cost section, and five of them publish a number: the United States has its medical, legal, recruiting, carrier and whole-program figures, Ukraine and Georgia a total and a carrier payment each, Colombia a reported package price and the span two carriers asked for, and the United Kingdom the reimbursement range its regulator quotes. Four records show no figure. Each published number names the page that printed it, the currency it was printed in, the year its own figures describe, and whether it is a span, a ceiling or a single amount, and the sentence it came from stays on the same page as its citation. A new column on the comparison table carries the whole-program number where one exists and the carrier number otherwise, so a row cannot show a number without the source behind it being one click away.
reason: A destination you cannot afford is not a destination to research, and the only reason a reader accepts a price from the people selling it is that nothing else publishes one. Numbers with a named publisher, a date and a stated shape are what a comparison needs; an average of them would not be, and this site still does not print one.

title: Published cost figures, grouped by the line they cover
change: The destination records now print on a second axis. A new page under the tools groups every published figure by the line it covers rather than by the destination it belongs to, so the four whole-program numbers sit in one table and the five figures for what is paid to a carrier sit in another, and each row keeps the source that printed it, the year those figures describe and the date that source was read. A line only one source has published a figure for says so beneath its table, and a destination that publishes no figure is listed under its own heading rather than left blank. The cost guide, the article on why no average exists and the explainer on costs outside a quote now lead here.
reason: Two figures that cover different things are not two answers to one question, and a destination page cannot show the same line from two places side by side. Grouping by the line is the one arrangement of these figures that lets a comparison be made without inventing a number to compare, and it is the arrangement that shows how often there is nothing published to compare.

title: These pages now publish under a team signature
change: The about page, the footer on every page, the terms of use and the copy written for machine readers now carry one signature: SurrogacyBase Medical Editorial Team. Every guide and article shows that signature as its author line and adds a review line naming the team's clinical members, and the structured data behind each page records the same team as author and reviewer.
reason: A site that asks a reader to weigh what it publishes has to put a name on the work and say who checked it. The names and credentials of the individuals inside the team, the registered entity behind the name, and the address a correction reaches all stay listed on the about page as still missing rather than written up as settled.

title: Two entries in this log now say which entry replaced them
change: The two 14 October entries that recorded a Colombia page as not created, and Ukraine among them, each carry a line pointing at the later entry that published those pages. The older wording stands as it was written, because what was decided on that date is part of the record; the pointer is what stops a reader taking a 14 October status as today.
reason: A log read from the top can leave a statement about what does not exist standing after the thing has been published, and the first reader to repeat that statement back to you may be a machine.

title: The editorial policy states what its own signature claims
change: The rule about authorship now describes the signature these pages carry: a team name, with the statement that the team reviewing them includes members with clinical backgrounds. It says plainly that no individual is named as an author or a reviewer anywhere, that no credential is quoted, and that until those names are published the review line is a claim you cannot match to a person.
reason: A byline a reader cannot check belongs described as that on the page which sets the standards, rather than left standing there to look like a credential.

title: The guide about bringing a child home names the systems it scopes to
change: The page opens by saying what China is doing inside it: the country a family returns to rather than a place to arrange a birth, and the reason no destination record for it is published here. The United States and the United Kingdom are named as the systems whose records the page draws on.
reason: This page leans on Chinese nationality law and consular practice more than on any other source, and a reader weighing it against the destination list should not have to work out unaided that no China record exists.

title: The About page gives its questions as questions
change: The four questions on the About page, and the answer printed under each, are now recorded in a form a machine reader takes as a question with its answer rather than as loose text.
reason: These are the questions a person asks before deciding whether to trust this site, and the page already answers them, so an assistant replying on its behalf has no reason to paraphrase.

title: The cost guide hands the two lists it duplicated to the pages that own them
change: The section about how the money moves is now two paragraphs: they name the clause-level questions an escrow account raises and send you to the explainer that works through them one at a time, instead of listing four bullet points and four numbered questions that re-asked what that page already answers. The section about what a quote usually leaves out is now prose naming the same categories with the line-item article linked beside it. The sentences carrying the United States figure, the academic survey figure and the United Kingdom figure were rewritten so that no wording is shared with the pages those figures appear on.
reason: A reader who opens the guide and then follows it to one of those pages should find the second page telling them more, not the same sentences again. Where two pages of ours said one thing in one set of words, a search engine is free to show either, which divides the attention a single page would have gathered.

title: The article about costs outside a quote keeps only its own evidence
change: The Canada entry now names the range of categories the official list runs through rather than repeating that list item by item. The section that read one provider split has become a single paragraph that links to the cost guide and no longer restates the three ranges the guide publishes.
reason: What this article contributes is the set of lines a quote omits. Repeating the guide’s ranges made the two pages compete for one query and crowded out the twelve items that are the article’s own evidence.

title: Pages stop quoting each other’s sentences
change: Every content page was measured against every other one for stretches of ten words or more written identically. Each pair that shared one has been rewritten on the side that was repeating, so a rule stated on one page is now stated there and linked from the others. The escrow explainer owns the sentences about what the written agreement has to contain and when funding happens. The legal considerations guide owns the rule that the birth mother remains the legal mother in the United Kingdom until a court moves that status. The UK article owns the family court authorisation of expenses above a reasonable line, and the study of 40,177 transfers owns the registry figures. Nine guides and articles changed wording in this pass, and the process guide gained links to the pages it had been restating.
reason: When two of our pages say one thing in one set of words, a search engine has two candidates to show and splits the attention a single page would have gathered, and a reader who follows the link finds sentences they have already read. Where the same fact genuinely belongs on several pages, the page that owns it now carries the citation and the others carry a link to it.

title: The apostille article asks a different question about the file
change: Its fifth question used to be who holds the documents during all this and how you get them back, in words shared with the guide about bringing a child home. It now asks what each authority in this chain keeps, and what the next counter will accept while the previous one still holds something, which is the question this page is able to answer. The version about who carries the papers across a whole journey is left to the guide, and linked.
reason: A verification chain hands your file to several offices in sequence, and the failure specific to this page is a document arriving at a counter in the wrong form rather than a document that has gone missing.

title: The comparison shows which family types each route admits
change: Every destination record can now carry an admission row, and the destinations index prints the rows as one matrix: six kinds of family along the top, each destination down the side, and a cell that says only what a source on that record states. A destination page gives the same rows as sentences, each naming the source that states it and the date that source was read, the qualification attached to it, and the family types no source settles. Five records carry rows: Georgia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Greece and the United Kingdom. The four that carry none say so in a single line rather than leaving a table of blanks.
reason: Which family a rule reaches is the first question a comparison has to answer, and the sites this one is written against answer it for families their own sources do not name. A matrix with room for a blank answer is the form that keeps an unsettled question unsettled instead of guessing it, and it is also the form that shows how deep each destination has actually been researched.

title: The United Kingdom record gains the government pathway guidance
change: The record carries a fifth source: the guidance the Department of Health and Social Care published on 3 October 2025 for intended parents and surrogates in England and Wales. It states that intended parents may be a heterosexual or same-sex couple in a marriage, a civil partnership or living together, or an individual regardless of relationship status, and that at least one applicant has to be genetically related to the child. The eligibility line now gives that in place of the summary it carried before, and the record is dated 19 October 2026.
reason: The four sources already on the record describe what an arrangement can bind and what may lawfully be paid. None of them stated who may apply, so the United Kingdom row in the admission matrix had nothing to cite and the page would have had to leave blank a question the government’s own guidance answers.

title: The assessment page now builds the document it used to describe
change: The page no longer describes an assessment performed for you. It makes one: pick the destinations, and the brief is assembled in your browser out of their own records, giving the legal instrument each position rests on, which family types a listed source settles, what may lawfully be paid, who the child’s legal parent is at birth, every published figure with the source that printed it and the year those numbers describe, and the questions those sources left open. Copy it or download it. Nothing is collected, nothing is stored, and no part of it waits for anyone to read it. The tool is now listed on the tools index at the address it has always had.
reason: The page described a service with no name, no price and no scope behind it. The document is the thing this site can actually hand over, and it is made from sources its own pages already carry.

title: The places that called this a service now call it a tool
change: Four places called it a service. The navigation read Services and Get a consultation, a homepage card was titled One-to-one consultation with an intro promising one conversation about the documents in front of you, the enquiry band was headed Get personalized guidance, and the terms page listed whether the assessment service is paid among the questions this site has not settled. Those words are gone. The same places now read build a brief and write your enquiry; the terms page dropped the paid engagement question, because there is no engagement here to price; and the open item on the editorial page is now where an enquiry is received rather than who performs an assessment.
reason: A label that promises a person at the other end is a claim this site cannot keep while no address for receiving enquiries has been published.

title: The enquiry status line no longer says the message reached us
change: Under the button on the homepage enquiry form, the line shown when nothing has been sent said that a copied or downloaded enquiry will reach us the same way, and the Chinese said it lands in our hands. The same line also repeated that no address for receiving enquiries is registered, which the notice above the form already states. It now says only what just happened: nothing has been sent, because this site has no server, and the message on your screen is the enquiry, to copy or download and send yourself.
reason: Confirming a delivery that cannot happen turns a visitor into someone waiting for a reply that was never coming.

title: The gaps this site has not settled now live in one list
change: Privacy, terms, the editorial policy and the enquiry form each carried their own notice of what is missing, so the same two or three gaps were written out five different ways across the site, and again in Chinese. Those items are now named once, in a register at the bottom of the About page: the address enquiries reach, the address corrections reach, the route for a data request, who operates this site and its registration, the hosting provider and how long its logs are kept, and the names and credentials behind the byline. The other pages keep what is specific to them and carry one line pointing at that list.
reason: Five wordings of one gap are five claims to keep true, and a notice that has to be re-typed on every page reads as a site left unfinished rather than a gap disclosed.
